title: Alypius at the games (6.8)
hook: his friend swears he'll keep his eyes shut and is caught by the roar
tomorrow: who does the book send away, and never name?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ambrose reading silently, eyes on the page and voice at rest. The line was reading in silence.

Thumb over the screen, scrolling fast past the fight video, promising yourself you won't watch. Then the comments explode. Augustine's friend Alypius made that promise in Rome, where he'd gone to study law. Friends coming from dinner dragged him, laughing, to the gladiator shows, which he hated. You can drag my body there, he told them, but not my mind or my eyes. He sat down and shut his eyes. Could he keep them shut when the whole arena roared?
screen: `THUMB OVER THE SCREEN.` → `DRAGGED TO THE GAMES.` → `EYES SHUT. THEN THE ROAR.`

segments.voice: No. Someone fell in the fight, the crowd let out a huge shout, and curiosity won. He opened his eyes, sure he could look down on whatever he saw. Augustine says he took a deeper wound in his soul than the fighter took in his body. He didn't turn away. He fixed his eyes, shouted, burned, and carried home a madness that drew him back again. So why didn't his promise hold? Augustine's answer is plain: Alypius trusted his own strength, when he should have trusted God. And he doesn't leave his friend there; God later pulled Alypius out, he says, and taught him that trust. A neighbor tradition sees the same danger. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, pictures someone who lives looking for pleasures, senses unguarded: the tempter throws him down the way wind throws down a weak tree. The one who guards the senses stands like a rocky mountain. Both say don't take the seat and count on your eyes. And one honest difference. For Augustine, the strength that finally held was God's, not Alypius's own. The Dhammapada puts the work in your own hands: self, it says, is the lord of self. One danger, two maps for crossing it.
screen: `A DEEPER WOUND THAN THE FIGHTER'S.` · `HE TRUSTED HIS OWN STRENGTH.` · `THE DHAMMAPADA: GUARD THE SENSES.` · `GOD'S STRENGTH, OR SELF AS LORD.` · then, large: `THE ROAR.`

segments.voice: Before the sit begins, do one small thing: put your phone face down across the room, or close the tab that tends to pull you in. That's the seat, moved. Then sit with the space it leaves, and notice how the pull feels from farther away.
Alypius at the games. Augustine's friend swore his eyes would stay shut, trusted his own strength, and one roar did the rest.
The line to keep: the roar, which he didn't choose, though he chose the seat. Rest easy.
